$comment: Property contract for the two production Compose models, enforced by
scripts/check-compose-invariants.mjs (issue #631).
Each row asserts one property of ONE model against the rendered output of
`docker compose config --no-interpolate`. There is deliberately no
model-to-model diff: docker-compose.prod.yml and docker-compose.release.yml
are two products (source build + cloudflared tunnel + manual migration, vs.
an immutable image bundle with its own migrate service), so nearly every
field would differ legitimately and the allowlist absolving them would be
indistinguishable from no check at all.
`why` is required on every row and must cite an issue, because the value
alone never says why it may not change. A row whose `path` no longer
resolves is a failure, not a pass -- otherwise a row left behind after a
refactor would silently stop guarding anything. Every service in a rendered
model must also be named by at least one row, so adding a service without
saying what governs it fails rather than slipping in ungoverned.
NOT assertable here: the top-level `name:` key. The checker renders with
`-p near-chat` to keep prod's project, network and volume names off the
checkout directory name, and `-p` overrides the file's own `name:` -- so a
row asserting it would pass even with the key deleted. It is asserted from
the source YAML instead, in backend/tests/unit/deploy/releaseComposeRuntime.test.ts.
expect: a literal to deep-equal, or {"$absent": true},
{"$matches": "<regex>"}, {"$keys": [...]} for an exact key set,
{"$every": {...}} for a non-empty list whose every element carries those
key/values, or {"$contains": {...}} for a list with at least one such
element. Indexing one element (ports[0]) is deliberately avoided for lists
that can grow: it says nothing about a second entry added after it.

invariants.why: #631: the service set is the frame every other prod row is written against. A service added or renamed without updating this contract would otherwise be governed by nothing.

#631: cloudflared is the only ingress (docker-compose.prod.yml:1-9). A database reachable off-host bypasses the tunnel entirely, and this binding is also what makes trusting X-Forwarded-For safe -- see TRUST_PROXY_HOPS below.

#631: same loopback-only ingress rule. Published on 0.0.0.0 the API would be reachable without the tunnel, and TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=1 would then let any caller forge X-Forwarded-For and choose its own rate-limit bucket (#413).
#631: same loopback-only ingress rule; the documented local production walkthrough browses http://localhost:3005 and needs nothing wider.
#631: this Redis has no password, so reachability from the compose network only IS its access control (docker-compose.prod.yml:29-34). Publishing any host port for it is never the right fix.
#631: cloudflared dials out to Cloudflare and accepts nothing inbound; a published port on it would be a second, unauthenticated ingress.

#631: exactly one trusted hop (cloudflared), pinned as a literal rather than ${TRUST_PROXY_HOPS:-1} on purpose (docker-compose.prod.yml:78-84) -- a value inherited from a shared .env would silently replace the default and funnel every caller into one rate-limit bucket (#413).

#631: single-dash `-`, not `:-`. An explicitly empty REDIS_URL must reach the container empty so the backend runs realtime single-node, which is a supported deployment rather than a value to default away (#471).

#631: pass-through with no `=`, so an unset LOG_LEVEL stays absent in the container and the logger applies its own default. Rewriting it as LOG_LEVEL= would set it to the empty string, which is a different thing.
#631: pass-through, like LOG_LEVEL. Unset means the backend generates one per process; an empty string is not the same input and would not round-trip through presence lease reclaim (#586).

#586: the drain in src/index.ts has a ~14s worst case and arms a 20s deadline. Docker's 10s default SIGKILLs the process while it is handing presence leases back, leaving users showing online until PRESENCE_TTL_MS expires.

#631: started, not healthy. src/utils/redis.ts treats Redis as a degraded mode rather than a boot dependency, so gating on its healthcheck would let a Redis that cannot bind stop the API serving routes that never touch Redis.
#558: prod builds from source, and this is the only production Dockerfile CI builds. Pointing it at the dev Dockerfile would ship a dev image under a production stack name.
#631: the tunnel is the only ingress, so it must come back after a host reboot without anyone running a command. `unless-stopped` would leave it down after an operator stops it once.

#631: single `$`, so Compose interpolates these host-side before the container sees them. prod's db reads POSTGRES_USER from the host .env, so a `$$` escape here would send the literal string to pg_isready and the healthcheck would never pass.
#631: the two stateful volumes. A renamed volume silently starts an empty one, which for pgdata means an empty database and for app_uploads means every existing attachment 404s.

#631: a top-level `pgdata:` declaration only says the volume exists. Deleting the mount, or moving its target off PGDATA, leaves the declaration in place and the database running on the container filesystem -- so every rebuild starts an empty database while the contract still passes.
#631: same gap as pgdata. Without this mount every uploaded attachment lives in the container layer and 404s after the next rebuild, with the app_uploads declaration still present and unused.
#631: the service set is the frame every other release row is written against, and `migrate` in particular is what makes the bundle self-applying (#558).

#558: the release bundle ships no source. A `build:` here would make the bundle silently rebuild from whatever happened to be in the extraction directory instead of running the image the release published.
#558: same -- the frontend image is published by the release workflow and must not be rebuilt at deploy time.
#527: digest-pinned so the bundle is reproducible. A floating tag means two deployments of the same release can run different Postgres builds.
#631: `:?` so a deployment missing BACKEND_IMAGE fails at render rather than booting something unintended. Unlike prod, the bundle has no source to fall back on.
#558: migrate must run the same image as the backend, or migrations execute against a schema built by a different version of the code.
#631: same fail-fast rule as BACKEND_IMAGE.

#631: `$$` escapes the interpolation so the container's own shell expands it. Written with a single `$` Compose would substitute host-side, and the credentials would be baked into the rendered config rather than read from the container environment.
#558: migrate is a run-once job. Any restart policy turns a failed migration into a crash loop that re-runs it forever instead of stopping the deployment.
#558: migrations must not start against a Postgres that is still initializing, or the run fails on a connection refused that looks like a bad migration.
#558: the backend must not boot against a schema migrate has not finished applying. Anything weaker lets the API serve requests mid-migration.

#413: this bundle publishes the backend port directly, so callers arrive as themselves and the peer address is the right thing to bucket on. Defaulting above 0 here would let any caller forge X-Forwarded-For.
#527: the bundle ships no Redis of its own, so this is empty by default and the backend runs realtime single-node -- a supported deployment, not a misconfiguration.
#631: `:?` so a bundle deployed without a database URL fails at render instead of booting and failing per-request.
#631: `:?` so the bundle cannot boot with an empty signing secret, which would make every issued token forgeable.
#631: `:?` rather than a permissive default. A blank origin list defaulted to `*` would let any site drive the API with a user's credentials.

#631: unlike prod, the release bundle publishes no database port at all. The backend reaches it over the compose network, and an exposed Postgres on a real deployment host is directly reachable from the internet.

#631: intentionally public, unlike prod's loopback binding -- this bundle has no bundled reverse proxy, so publishing directly is how it is reached. Recorded so the difference reads as a deliberate choice rather than drift, and so pairing it with a non-zero TRUST_PROXY_HOPS fails this contract.
#631: same -- the bundle publishes the frontend directly.
#631: the bundle is the unattended deployment path, so its long-running services come back after a host reboot without an operator.
#631: same as db. Note migrate deliberately differs -- see its own row.
#631: same as db and backend.
#586: same drain budget as prod -- Docker's 10s default SIGKILLs the backend while it is handing presence leases back.
#631: the same two stateful volumes as prod. A rename in the bundle silently starts an empty database on an upgrade of an existing deployment.

#631: as in prod, the top-level declaration is not the mount. On the bundle this is worse: an upgrade that drops the mount discards a real deployment's database rather than a local test one, and the unused declaration keeps the contract looking satisfied.
#631: as in prod -- without the mount every attachment uploaded to a deployment is lost on the next image bump.
